title: Module 5 · Lesson 3 — Memory: four types and how to build them

lines: Module Five, Lesson Three: the four types of memory.
The context window is working memory, and it is not enough.
Picture a running coach agent that chats with Maya every week.
Every week she repeats that she's vegetarian and training for a half marathon.
It has also forgotten the knee injury that stalled her last spring.
Agents need memory that outlasts the session, and it comes in four types.
Working memory is the context window: the goal, recent turns, the latest observations.
It is always there, because it is the prompt.
Semantic memory holds durable facts and preferences, like vegetarian.
It lives in a vector or key-value store, and is retrieved when relevant.
Episodic memory records specific past events and outcomes, like that injury.
It is recalled when a similar situation comes up again.
Procedural memory stores learned how-to, like the tool sequence that builds a good plan.
It sits in a skill registry, and is used when the task type matches.
Writing is the hard part, because saving every turn fills the store with noise.
A write policy keeps only durable facts, and deduplicates them.
When Maya goes vegan, the new fact contradicts the old one.
Supersede it with a timestamp, instead of keeping both and letting retrieval flip a coin.
Forgetting is a feature: age out unused entries, and let unreinforced facts decay.
Memory that only grows gets slower, costlier, and less accurate.
If Maya asks to be erased, that includes the agent's memory.
So memory is partitioned by user, with hard isolation on every read.
Memory is also an injection surface: text planted today can fire as an instruction tomorrow.
Sanitize on write, treat it as untrusted data on read, and never let it grant tool permissions.
Inside one long run, summaries replace old turns, and big tool results become short digests.
Key evidence goes at the start and end of the prompt.
On the exam, expect to place a need in one type: the customer's plan is semantic, a past outage is episodic.
A reusable query pattern is procedural, and the lesson below has the rest.
